To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the treatment of childhood cancer is associated with a variety of late CNS effects, including radioncrosis, leukoencepholapathy, cerebellar dysfunction, neurocognitive and neuroendocrinological dysfunction and secondary CNS neoplasms.

(1) long-term survivors of childhood cancer are at increased risk of CNS damage, (2) radiotherapy and, to a lesser extent methotrexate are implicated as causes of such damage, (3) the pathogenesis of CNS sequelae is incompletely understood, (4) neurocognitive dysfunction, growth hormone insufficiency and secondary tumors are the most common forms of CNS sequelae, (5) younger children and children with CNS tumors are at increased risk, and (6
the long-term sequelae of CNS irradiation in children include neurocognitive and neuroendocrinological deficits and that these deficits are progressive.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effects of CNS-directed therapy on the developing brain.
the effects of radiotherapy on the central nervous systems of childhood.
the study of the pathogenesis and clinical manifestations of CNS sequelae in long-term survivors of childhood cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
long-term survivors of childhood cancer have an increased risk of developing neurologic, neurocognitive and neuroendocrinological dysfunction.
CNS damage may occur after treatment of childhood cancer, the exact etiology is not completely understood, and the frequency, degree and nature of damage is difficult to determine.
the long-term effects of treatment on the CNS are not fully understood and the full extent of the damage may be underestimated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the long-term sequelae of treatment of CNS tumors and other malignancies in childhood may be significant and that further research is necessary to define the extent of these sequelae and the means of preventing and/or ameliorating them.
we are only just beginning to understand the effects of CNS treatment on the long-term survivor.
the CNS is at risk for long-term damage from cancer treatment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have to be aware of these long-term sequelae and we have to try to do something about them.
we need to be more aggressive in our efforts to detect and treat the sequelae of cancer therapy on the central nervous systems of children with cancer.
we need to be more aggressive with our efforts to prevent and treat these complications of cancer treatment.
